Despite the abundance of seven-figure homes, Cobble Hill has small-town vibe evident in the mom-and-pop stores and Italian influences that dot Court Street. Walk down the sunny commercial strip and you'll pass the local butcher, the baker and the fishmonger — all family-run and equally popular among local residents and foodies from far and wide. Its waterfront is now lined with upscale, glassy new developments aimed at young professionals who seek luxury amenities and convenient access to Midtown. In 2018, Amazon chose this neighborhood as the site for one of its two new East Coast hubs, which means some industrial buildings and pothole-pocked streets will almost certainly give way to a gleaming new tech campus. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $899K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,100 When many people think of the Upper East Side, they think of a quiet, tree-lined urban expanse filled with posh residents and purebred dogs. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. And the eastern side of the neighborhood, toward Yorkville, exhibits a less rarefied character. Second Avenue is home to sports bars, pubs, and some excellent restaurants. A trendy renaissance is in the offing here, sparked by young professionals drawn by some surprisingly good housing prices (for Manhattan). The avenues and commerce-lined thoroughfares can be hectic, but many streets on the Upper East Side are blessedly quiet — just one more way in which this oft-stereotyped neighborhood can be a surprise. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $950K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,325 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,999 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. A trendy renaissance is in the offing here, sparked by young professionals drawn by some surprisingly good housing prices (for Manhattan). Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 3 beds $2.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 3 beds $6,300 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $899K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,650 Bisected by Flatbush Avenue and bordered by the BQE, Downtown Brooklyn is a rapidly expanding residential neighborhood. Easy subway access and abundant inventory have drawn many to the area looking for luxury rentals and condos in the area's numerous new apartment towers. Historically, Downtown Brooklyn has been the hub of the borough's municipal activities with many civil service offices and court houses centered around Cadman Plaza, the neighborhood's main hub. With tons of city employees, lawyers and Brooklynites of all types constantly bustling about, Downtown Brooklyn has a decidedly hectic vibe. This, coupled with the area's lack of green space, makes Downtown Brooklyn most appealing to those who can embrace one of Brooklyn's busiest and most trafficked neighborhoods. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,895 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,000 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. For that reason, it is a perennial favorite. The Upper West Side is relaxed, but never dull. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $900K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,275 When many people think of the Upper East Side, they think of a quiet, tree-lined urban expanse filled with posh residents and purebred dogs. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. And the eastern side of the neighborhood, toward Yorkville, exhibits a less rarefied character. Second Avenue is home to sports bars, pubs, and some excellent restaurants. A trendy renaissance is in the offing here, sparked by young professionals drawn by some surprisingly good housing prices (for Manhattan). The avenues and commerce-lined thoroughfares can be hectic, but many streets on the Upper East Side are blessedly quiet — just one more way in which this oft-stereotyped neighborhood can be a surprise. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,000 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,895 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $2M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $8,295 When many people think of the Upper East Side, they think of a quiet, tree-lined urban expanse filled with posh residents and purebred dogs. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. And the eastern side of the neighborhood, toward Yorkville, exhibits a less rarefied character. Second Avenue is home to sports bars, pubs, and some excellent restaurants. A trendy renaissance is in the offing here, sparked by young professionals drawn by some surprisingly good housing prices (for Manhattan). The avenues and commerce-lined thoroughfares can be hectic, but many streets on the Upper East Side are blessedly quiet — just one more way in which this oft-stereotyped neighborhood can be a surprise. Sales Median asking price 3 beds $3.6M Rentals Median asking base rent 3 beds $35,000 When many people think of the Upper East Side, they think of a quiet, tree-lined urban expanse filled with posh residents and purebred dogs. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. And the eastern side of the neighborhood, toward Yorkville, exhibits a less rarefied character. Second Avenue is home to sports bars, pubs, and some excellent restaurants. A trendy renaissance is in the offing here, sparked by young professionals drawn by some surprisingly good housing prices (for Manhattan). The avenues and commerce-lined thoroughfares can be hectic, but many streets on the Upper East Side are blessedly quiet — just one more way in which this oft-stereotyped neighborhood can be a surprise. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 3 beds $2.74M Rentals Median asking base rent 3 beds $7,650 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,895 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,895 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $812K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,150 Cobble Hill is a beautiful, historic neighborhood with some of the borough's most expensive real estate. Despite the abundance of seven-figure homes, Cobble Hill has small-town vibe evident in the mom-and-pop stores and Italian influences that dot Court Street. Walk down the sunny commercial strip and you'll pass the local butcher, the baker and the fishmonger — all family-run and equally popular among local residents and foodies from far and wide. On the side streets, the homes tend to be large brick townhouses and brownstones owned by single families, with well-kept facades and window boxes. This is a neighborhood where homeownership is a luxury, and residents take that responsibility to heart. The blocks are clean, the community associations active, and the lifestyle warm and genteel. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.62M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.62M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,795 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 3 beds $2.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 3 beds $6,300 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,972 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,997 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $2M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,300 Cobble Hill is a beautiful, historic neighborhood with some of the borough's most expensive real estate. Despite the abundance of seven-figure homes, Cobble Hill has small-town vibe evident in the mom-and-pop stores and Italian influences that dot Court Street. Walk down the sunny commercial strip and you'll pass the local butcher, the baker and the fishmonger — all family-run and equally popular among local residents and foodies from far and wide. On the side streets, the homes tend to be large brick townhouses and brownstones owned by single families, with well-kept facades and window boxes. This is a neighborhood where homeownership is a luxury, and residents take that responsibility to heart. The blocks are clean, the community associations active, and the lifestyle warm and genteel. Easy subway access and abundant inventory have drawn many to the area looking for luxury rentals and condos in the area's numerous new apartment towers. Historically, Downtown Brooklyn has been the hub of the borough's municipal activities with many civil service offices and court houses centered around Cadman Plaza, the neighborhood's main hub. With tons of city employees, lawyers and Brooklynites of all types constantly bustling about, Downtown Brooklyn has a decidedly hectic vibe. This, coupled with the area's lack of green space, makes Downtown Brooklyn most appealing to those who can embrace one of Brooklyn's busiest and most trafficked neighborhoods. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,895 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,999 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,972 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,997 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $2M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,250 Cobble Hill is a beautiful, historic neighborhood with some of the borough's most expensive real estate. Despite the abundance of seven-figure homes, Cobble Hill has small-town vibe evident in the mom-and-pop stores and Italian influences that dot Court Street. Walk down the sunny commercial strip and you'll pass the local butcher, the baker and the fishmonger — all family-run and equally popular among local residents and foodies from far and wide. On the side streets, the homes tend to be large brick townhouses and brownstones owned by single families, with well-kept facades and window boxes. This is a neighborhood where homeownership is a luxury, and residents take that responsibility to heart. The blocks are clean, the community associations active, and the lifestyle warm and genteel. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $899K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,650 Bisected by Flatbush Avenue and bordered by the BQE, Downtown Brooklyn is a rapidly expanding residential neighborhood. Easy subway access and abundant inventory have drawn many to the area looking for luxury rentals and condos in the area's numerous new apartment towers. Historically, Downtown Brooklyn has been the hub of the borough's municipal activities with many civil service offices and court houses centered around Cadman Plaza, the neighborhood's main hub. With tons of city employees, lawyers and Brooklynites of all types constantly bustling about, Downtown Brooklyn has a decidedly hectic vibe. This, coupled with the area's lack of green space, makes Downtown Brooklyn most appealing to those who can embrace one of Brooklyn's busiest and most trafficked neighborhoods. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $899K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,650 Bisected by Flatbush Avenue and bordered by the BQE, Downtown Brooklyn is a rapidly expanding residential neighborhood. Easy subway access and abundant inventory have drawn many to the area looking for luxury rentals and condos in the area's numerous new apartment towers. Historically, Downtown Brooklyn has been the hub of the borough's municipal activities with many civil service offices and court houses centered around Cadman Plaza, the neighborhood's main hub. With tons of city employees, lawyers and Brooklynites of all types constantly bustling about, Downtown Brooklyn has a decidedly hectic vibe. This, coupled with the area's lack of green space, makes Downtown Brooklyn most appealing to those who can embrace one of Brooklyn's busiest and most trafficked neighborhoods. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,972 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 3 beds $2.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 3 beds $6,300 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,900 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.6M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $6,500 Sandwiched between two beautiful parks, the Upper West Side is one of the greenest spots in Manhattan. For that reason, it is a perennial favorite. The Upper West Side is relaxed, but never dull. There are plenty of low-key bars and restaurants to frequent along Amsterdam Avenue, and Broadway is an always-bustling commercial center. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.6M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $6,400 Sandwiched between two beautiful parks, the Upper West Side is one of the greenest spots in Manhattan. For that reason, it is a perennial favorite. The Upper West Side is relaxed, but never dull. There are plenty of low-key bars and restaurants to frequent along Amsterdam Avenue, and Broadway is an always-bustling commercial center. The wide, tree-lined streets still boast many mom-and-pop stores. Less posh than the Upper East Side, it is more easily accessible by public transportation, and real estate prices are just as, if not more, expensive. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $950K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,325 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,895 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. And the eastern side of the neighborhood, toward Yorkville, exhibits a less rarefied character. Second Avenue is home to sports bars, pubs, and some excellent restaurants. A trendy renaissance is in the offing here, sparked by young professionals drawn by some surprisingly good housing prices (for Manhattan). The avenues and commerce-lined thoroughfares can be hectic, but many streets on the Upper East Side are blessedly quiet — just one more way in which this oft-stereotyped neighborhood can be a surprise. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,950 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $925K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,395 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Strollers and children of all ages are a constant presence on sidewalks, as are shoppers patronizing local boutiques and dog walkers heading up to the park. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699.5K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,850 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,999 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.62M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,000 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,900 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,995 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.65M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,400 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,000 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,000 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.3M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $5,000 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block.
